RR Auction has concluded the auction of a science fair project created by late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs in 1968, with the handmade exhibit ultimately selling for $34,375. Details below.

"Overall condition is excellent to near mint"

Earlier, we reported that a science fair project created by Jobs in 1968, during his sophomore year of high school, was up for auction.

The project examined silicon-controlled rectifiers and included two demonstration circuits as well as a 10-page report. At the time, online bids had not yet surpassed $3,000.

The auction was part of "Jobs and the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part II." Bidding has now ended, and according to MacRumors, which first reported the result, the final sale price reached $34,375.

According to RR Auction, the exhibit "had been kept for years at the famed 'Apple Garage' property" and was carefully preserved by Jobs's family. Jobs's stepbrother, John Chovanec, said that Jobs repeatedly refused to take the exhibit back, ultimately allowing Chovanec to keep it.

"Jobs and the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction Part II" featured nearly 150 Apple- and technology-related treasures, including a business card personally signed by Jobs, a collection of electronic components from his personal collection, and a letter in which he declined a speaking invitation in 1983. These lots sold for $156,658, $27,188, and $24,695 respectively.

The highest-selling lot in the auction was a working Apple-1 computer, one of the second batch of 50 units, which ultimately went for $499,363.
